Hi, good afternoon. We're delighted to have Karl Stang with us, who's the acting executive director of the World Food Program. He just spoke to the council. We'll say a few words and we'll take a few questions. Karl.

Thank you, Stefan. Today I brought to the council what WFP frontline teams are witnessing every day. I've also had opportunity to visit many of those operations. So I spoke to the council about how hunger and conflict really looks in practice, how that cycle of hunger and conflict looks in practice, drawing from that firsthand experience during my visits, and that how this vicious cycle is now escalating, and that waiting for a famine being declared is a total failure of duty. It should be a wake-up call for all, because when families don't have food to put on the table, they only have three choices or three options, and they're all terrible. Starve, move, or rebel. Today, I also flagged a new dimension, that the double choking point that many have been speaking about, the Hormuz and the Red Sea, is now a triple choking point, adding the escalation in the Black Sea. How many more choking points can the world really muster before it completely suffocates? I also wanted to show though what is possible if there is political will. And I call on the Security Council to take urgent and concrete action to break this cycle of hunger and conflict. I suggested five circuit breakers. First, measures that stop conflict in one region. to drive hunger in another. Second, to act early. As I said, when famines are declared, it's already way too late. Three, to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. Four, to protect humanitarian personnel. And five, and fifth, solidarity with the most vulnerable in the world. The current funding cuts to our programs is simply not sustainable. I used to talk about taking food from the hungry to give to the starving. But in some context right now, we are on the verge of having nothing to give at all. We all risk becoming bystanders as children starve. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Mr. Skow. You and I were both here during the last Somali almost famine starting, and there was a great outpouring that actually kept it from happening and becoming greater. You started your speech to the Security Council talking about the difference in six years from the time that WFP won the Nobel Peace Prize until today. Well, WFP We refuse to accept that hunger, uh, is being normalized, but it is indeed true that we have seen, uh, a dramatic deterioration in the situation, as I spoke to today, back in 2018, when… 2417, this resolution that we today speak to was adopted, and then in 2020, when WFP was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, there was a lot of hope, you know, at WFP, a lot of optimism. We really thought that eradicating hunger, zero hunger was possible. But of course, fast-forwarding to today, only six years later, we have seen a tripling of needs, almost 300 million people acutely food insecure. I spoke today again about our team in northern Yemen. 38 of my colleagues there are still in detainment. Why that is, you know, I cannot respond to, but what I can say is that we refuse to accept that reality. You can count on WFP to do whatever we can, but that's why I was so clear to member states what they need to do, their responsibility in trying to break this vicious cycle.

Thank you so much. Your speech today, Mr. Skow, said really, it said it all. Very powerful speech, diagnoses the whole problem. You spoke also of political will. Well, in many capitals, I think, you know, The response is that there are domestic pressures that need to be dealt with.
